summary: User-facing security and privacy guide for a local-first Studio that opens untrusted cards, scripts, regex sets, PNGs, and archives. Your content stays under your control through a primary loopback listener, no accounts or telemetry, and plain inspectable studio files, while the guide names three deliberate network boundaries: provider-backed Kit turns, user-opened update and version-switch information, and explicitly enabled remote access. A card cannot run itself because regex is validated and budgeted, macros and triggers are analyzed, and Lua runs only in the opt-in Risu Test Bench with worker, WebAssembly, resource, and separate-origin defenses whose packaged-host isolation is not yet proven. The sandbox origin serves only the Lua worker, regex worker, and glue.wasm. Other files stay bounded by body, archive, parsing, and path rules. Converting never copies one app's code into another because only portable canonical content crosses formats while private fields stay escrowed. About API keys describes optional BYOP Kit vault storage, hop-by-hop provider destination checks, the missing non-Windows passphrase setup flow, and Studio's ephemeral mutation token.

sections.title: Your content stays under your control
sections.summary: Studio's primary listener binds the local-only 127.0.0.1 address, and Hoplight has no hosted account, telemetry, analytics, background content upload, or inference proxy. Canonical pieces remain readable JSON files under the chosen studio directory, making them portable and user-backupable but not encrypted at rest; anyone already able to read the user's files can read them. Network activity is deliberate and tied to visible actions: Kit sends model context to the configured provider when a turn is submitted, Updates reads fixed GitHub release endpoints during update or version-switch flows, and remote access creates only the separately enabled listener or tunnel after its approval flow. Import, editing, conversion, and deterministic analysis make no provider request.

sections.title: A card cannot run itself
sections.summary: Downloaded content is parsed rather than automatically executed. Regex rules are budgeted find-and-replace data, never eval; structurally dangerous patterns are rejected before execution because a timeout cannot reliably interrupt one pathological native match. Macros and Risu-style triggers are analyzed without evaluation, including calc expressions handled by a small numeric parser. Lua executes only after the user opens the Risu Test Bench, never during import, preview, or background work. The bench uses real Lua in WebAssembly inside a killable worker with time and memory limits, served from a second loopback origin that exposes only the Lua worker, regex worker, and glue.wasm, with no session token or API. HTTP-layer tests prove that boundary, but packaged Windows-host isolation remains unmeasured, so the guide claims opt-in limitation rather than complete isolation.

sections.title: Other files stay bounded
sections.summary: Untrusted files are constrained before they can consume unbounded memory, corrupt state, or escape storage. Uploads and request bodies have hard size ceilings. ZIP and PNG readers enforce bounded extraction so compressed archive bombs stop at configured limits rather than expanding indefinitely. Parsers fail closed on malformed content instead of producing partially trusted entities. Kit's gated apply saves and re-reads its target to verify intended canonical content, while Studio editors send expected revisions so stale writes are rejected. Piece identifiers are validated and resolved strictly beneath the selected studio directory; crafted traversal names fail before filesystem access can escape that root.
topics: Kit read-back and Studio revision checks

sections.title: Converting never copies one app's code into another
sections.summary: Cross-format conversion carries only the portable canonical content understood by both sides. Source-specific extension blocks, layout data, triggers, and executable-looking payloads remain in the saved piece's escrow rather than being copied into another platform's output. That escrow allows same-format re-export to preserve source-owned information while preventing a conversion from smuggling one application's private code into a different application's file. Hoplight reports content that cannot cross instead of silently pretending it was portable. The rule is structural: the shared readable core converts, while platform-private material remains attached to its source format.

sections.title: About API keys
sections.summary: Provider-backed Kit is optional and uses bring-your-own-provider credentials; import, conversion, inspection, validation, editing, and deterministic checks continue without a key. Windows uses the operating-system credential backend. A portable passphrase-encrypted backend exists, but the current settings flow does not collect or supply the passphrase, so first-run setup and unlock remain incomplete on non-Windows systems. Credentials authenticate the configured provider and stay out of messages, tool observations, canonical pieces, exports, transcripts, and privacy accounting. Provider requests validate the configured host before every hop and refuse cross-host redirects, HTTPS downgrades, and chains beyond five redirects. Separately, Studio creates a fresh local session token at launch to authorize mutations and does not persist it.

sections.title: What we do not claim
sections.summary: The guide avoids reassuring but unsupported claims. Current desktop binaries are unsigned, so SmartScreen or Gatekeeper warnings are expected; users should verify the SHA-256 checksums shipped with releases rather than treating the warning alone as evidence of tampering. The separate Test Bench origin has automated HTTP-layer proof but has not been measured inside the packaged desktop host. Canonical studio files are intentionally readable and are not encrypted at rest. Kit's portable vault still lacks a settings-driven passphrase setup and unlock flow. Security reports should go privately to chibiconeja@gmail.com, also listed in SECURITY.md.
